buildUp: Start with the goal of one big screen you touch. That fixes the front: a sheet of glass, a touch sensor under it, a display under that, and one button to always get home.
Touching glass all day would scratch plastic, so the cover has to be hard, toughened glass, and a steel bezel round the edge takes the knocks.
The screen needs a computer to draw it smoothly, so a processor with graphics and memory goes on a small board, with flash storage for music and photos.
To be a phone and reach the internet it needs radios for the mobile network, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and their antennas must sit behind something that isn't metal.
Everything runs on a battery, which takes up most of the remaining space; the board is squeezed into the top half to make room for it.

Finally the details that make it feel effortless: sensors to rotate the picture and switch the screen off at your ear, a ring/silent switch you can feel, and a dock connector that works with existing iPod accessories.
firstPrinciples.coreIdea: Make almost the whole front a screen, and let your fingers act directly on what you see. If the controls are drawn in software instead of moulded in plastic, one slab of glass can become a keypad, a music player, a map or a web page, and it can change with every app. Everything else in the phone exists to make that screen sharp, responsive and alive for a whole day.

hardParts.title: Making touch feel instant and exact
hardParts.why: The sensor has to find several fingers precisely through glass, ignore your palm and stray electrical noise, and respond fast enough that scrolling feels attached to your fingertip. Old touchscreens needed a stylus and a firm press; doing this with light, imprecise fingers required both new sensing hardware and a lot of clever software.

hardParts.title: A glass screen that survives a pocket
hardParts.why: Plastic scratches and ordinary glass shatters. A plastic prototype screen got scratched by keys in a pocket, so Apple switched to a chemically toughened glass months before launch, with manufacturing that had to be scaled up almost from scratch.

hardParts.title: Fitting a day of use into a 5 Wh battery
hardParts.why: A desktop-style computer, a bright screen and several radios could easily drain the battery in a couple of hours. Getting to a day meant choosing low-power chips, running them slower than their maximum, and software that aggressively sleeps everything you're not using.

principles.explanation: The screen feels touch by measuring how your finger, a conductor, changes the charge on a grid of electrodes, so it can follow several fingers at once but not a stylus or glove. Your body holds electric charge, and a fingertip near a charged electrode changes how much charge it can store. A grid of clear electrodes under the glass measures that change at every crossing point many times a second. Because each crossing is measured separately, two touches never blur into one, which is what makes pinching possible. A stylus or a gloved finger doesn't carry charge the same way, so the grid barely notices it.
principles.title: Capacitance: your finger is a conductor

principles.explanation: The battery holds a fixed amount of energy, only about 5 watt-hours, so to last a day the phone has to keep its average power tiny. A battery's size is set by the room left over. The original iPhone's 5 watt-hours would run a 5-watt light bulb for only an hour. So when you're not touching it, the phone sleeps its processor, powers down radios and switches off the backlight. Every design choice, from a slower 412 MHz processor to leaving out 3G, comes back to this budget.
principles.title: Energy is the real budget

principles.explanation: Metal shields radio waves, so the antennas sit behind a black plastic strip at the bottom of the aluminium back. Radio waves are oscillating electric fields, and a conductor like aluminium lets electrons move to cancel them out, so a sealed metal box acts like a shield. An antenna inside one would barely talk to the network. Behind the strip, waves can get in and out.
principles.title: Metal blocks radio waves

principles.explanation: The LCD makes no light of its own; each pixel is a tiny liquid-crystal shutter that a voltage opens or closes in front of a backlight. A backlight shines through two polarising filters at right angles that would normally block everything, and between them a liquid crystal twists the light's polarisation by an amount set by a voltage. Twist it fully and the light passes; don't and it's blocked. Put red, green and blue filters over hundreds of thousands of these tiny shutters and you have a colour picture.
principles.title: Liquid crystals as light shutters

firstPrinciples.problem: Put a whole computer, a phone, a music player and the internet into something that fits in a pocket and runs all day on a battery, and make it simple enough that anyone can use it without a manual. Every part of that fights every other: a bigger screen means less room for battery, more speed means more heat and a flatter battery, and every extra button is one more thing to learn.

questions.answer: The touch sensor detects the change in electric charge caused by a conductive object near the glass. Your finger is conductive; a pencil's wood and most glove fabric aren't, so the sensor simply can't see them.
questions.question: Why couldn't you use the original iPhone's screen with a pencil or while wearing ordinary gloves?

questions.answer: Aluminium conducts electricity and blocks radio waves. The antennas sit behind the plastic strip so their signals can get out to the network and back.
questions.question: Why is the bottom of the back plastic rather than aluminium like the rest?

questions.answer: The 3G chips of 2007 used much more power, and the battery was the tightest constraint in the whole phone. Apple chose all-day battery life over faster data, then added 3G a year later when the chips improved.
questions.question: Why did Apple leave out the faster 3G network?

firstPrinciples.xFactor: The hardware was not far ahead of other phones; the leap was treating the whole front as one programmable surface and making the software feel physical. Lists that keep gliding and bounce at the end, pinch to zoom, and a keyboard that predicts which key you meant turned a sheet of glass into something that felt natural to touch. That decision is why almost every phone since looks like it.

name: Original iPhone
overview:
Apple's first iPhone, unveiled by Steve Jobs in January 2007 and on sale that June, is the phone that set the pattern for nearly every smartphone since: almost the whole front is a touchscreen, with a single button below it. Jobs introduced it as three devices in one, an iPod, a phone and an internet communicator.

The big idea was multi-touch. Instead of a stylus or a keyboard, a grid of transparent electrodes under the glass sensed several fingers at once, so you could pinch to zoom and flick through lists. Under the screen sits a small computer: an ARM processor running at 412 MHz with 128 MB of memory, 4 or 8 GB of flash storage, and separate chips for the phone network, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. Sensors turned the picture when you rotated the phone and switched the screen off when you held it to your ear.

By today's standards it was very limited: no 3G, no GPS, no App Store, a 2-megapixel camera that couldn't record video, and a battery soldered in place. The back shows how early it was. It is mostly aluminium, but radio waves can't pass through metal, so the bottom is a strip of black plastic that hides the antennas.

parts.description: Sheet of toughened glass over the whole front; Apple switched from plastic to glass just months before launch.

details.didYouKnow: Prototypes had a plastic screen until Steve Jobs found it scratched by the keys in his pocket, only months before launch. Apple turned to Corning, which revived a toughened glass it had shelved in the 1960s, the material later sold as Gorilla Glass.
details.howItWorks: The glass covers the whole front, from above the earpiece to below the home button, and is held at its edges by the steel bezel. It protects the touch sensor and screen beneath while letting your finger's electric field pass straight through, so the sensor can feel you without you ever touching it. A flat, hard surface also meant fingers could glide across it for scrolling and swiping.
details.madeOf: Chemically toughened glass from Corning, soaked in a hot bath of molten potassium salt so larger potassium ions pack into its surface and squeeze it into compression. That squeezed skin is what stops small scratches from growing into cracks.

parts.name: Front glass

parts.description: Grid of transparent electrodes that senses several fingers at once, the heart of pinch-to-zoom.

details.didYouKnow: Much of Apple's multi-touch know-how came from FingerWorks, a small company making gesture keyboards and trackpads, which Apple bought in 2005.
details.howItWorks: Rows and columns of transparent electrodes form a grid under the glass, and a controller chip measures the tiny electric charge between every crossing point many times a second. A fingertip draws away some of that charge, so the controller can map where each finger is, even several at once. That is what made pinch-to-zoom and two-finger gestures possible, where older touchscreens could only find one point, usually pressed with a stylus.
keyNumbers: Electrode lines far thinner than a hair are invisible to the eye
details.madeOf: Indium tin oxide, a metal oxide that conducts electricity yet is almost perfectly clear, patterned in thin lines on glass or plastic film. It is bonded under the front glass with clear adhesive.

parts.name: Multi-touch sensor

parts.description: Colour LCD of 320 by 480 pixels whose liquid crystals act as tiny shutters over a backlight.

details.didYouKnow: 163 pixels per inch was sharp for a phone in 2007, but three years later the iPhone 4's Retina display packed exactly twice as many pixels in each direction into the same size of screen.
details.howItWorks: Each pixel has a red, green and blue sub-pixel, and a layer of liquid crystal in front of each one twists the light from the backlight. Polarising filters on either side turn that twist into brightness, so the crystal works like a tiny shutter that a transistor opens or closes. Unlike an OLED, the LCD makes no light of its own, so even black pixels let a little backlight leak through.
keyNumbers: Over 150,000 pixels, each with three sub-pixels
details.madeOf: Liquid crystal sealed between two thin glass plates, one carrying a grid of thin-film transistors and the other the colour filters, sandwiched between polarising films.

parts.name: 3.5-inch LCD panel

parts.description: White LEDs along one edge and a clear plastic light guide that spreads their light evenly behind the LCD.

details.didYouKnow: A white LED is usually a blue LED in disguise: the yellow phosphor coating turns part of its blue light into yellow, and blue plus yellow looks white to the eye.
details.howItWorks: A row of tiny white LEDs shines into the edge of a thin sheet of clear plastic called a light guide. Tiny dots printed on its back scatter the light upwards, and diffuser and prism films on top spread it evenly and aim it towards your eyes. The ambient light sensor tells the phone how bright the room is, and the phone dims these LEDs to match.
keyNumbers: Typically a handful of LEDs along one edge
Often the biggest single power user while the screen is on
details.madeOf: White LEDs (blue LEDs coated with a yellow phosphor), an acrylic or polycarbonate light guide, and thin plastic diffuser and brightness-enhancing films, with a white reflector sheet underneath.

parts.name: LED backlight

parts.description: The single button on the front: one press always takes you back to the home screen.

details.didYouKnow: Phones of the time were covered in keys, so a single button below a big screen was one of the original iPhone's most surprising design choices. The button survived on iPhones until the iPhone X dropped it in 2017.
details.howItWorks: Pressing the button collapses a small metal dome switch on a flex cable underneath, which clicks and closes a circuit. Wherever you are, one press returns to the home screen, so you could never get lost; a double press could be set to open favourites or the iPod controls. The button simply moves and clicks, with no fingerprint sensor or touch sensing.
keyNumbers: The only button on the front
details.madeOf: A moulded plastic cap marked with a rounded square, sitting over a stainless steel dome switch. The dome springs back after each press.

parts.name: Home button

parts.description: Small speaker behind the slot above the screen that you hold to your ear on calls.

details.didYouKnow: On 2007's GSM networks, call audio was squeezed into a narrow band of frequencies, which is why phone voices sounded tinny however good the speaker was.
details.howItWorks: A small coil of wire sits in the field of a magnet and pushes a thin diaphragm back and forth as the voice signal changes, making sound you hear when you press the phone to your ear. It is tuned to play quietly and clearly at close range, unlike the loudspeaker on the bottom edge. A fine mesh behind the slot in the glass keeps out dust.
keyNumbers: Call audio covers about 300 Hz to 3.4 kHz on the networks of the time
Slot in the glass about 1 cm long
details.madeOf: A thin plastic diaphragm, a copper voice coil and a small neodymium magnet in a plastic housing.

parts.name: Earpiece speaker

parts.description: Infrared proximity sensor that turns the screen off against your cheek, and a light sensor that sets its brightness.

details.didYouKnow: The tinted window over the sensors looks black to you but is almost clear to infrared light, which is just beyond the red end of what our eyes can see.
details.howItWorks: The proximity sensor sends out a pulse of invisible infrared light and watches for a reflection; when your cheek comes close during a call, the reflection is strong and the phone switches off the touchscreen so you don't hang up with your ear. Beside it, an ambient light sensor measures how bright the room is so the phone can turn the backlight up outdoors and down in the dark.
keyNumbers: Detects a face a few centimetres away
Infrared wavelength of roughly 850 to 950 nm
details.madeOf: An infrared LED and a photodiode for proximity, plus a second photodiode for room light, packed in small plastic packages behind tinted windows in the glass that infrared passes through.

parts.name: Proximity & light sensors

parts.description: Polished stainless steel ring round the front that frames the glass and gives the phone its chrome edge.

details.didYouKnow: The polished steel ring echoed the shiny stainless steel backs of the iPods of the time, which were famous for picking up fine scratches almost as soon as they came out of the box.
details.howItWorks: The bezel wraps round the front edge and holds the glass and display in place against the case. Its raised lip sits slightly proud of the glass, so the phone lying face down on a table rests on metal rather than on the screen. It is purely structural and decorative; unlike the steel band on the iPhone 4, it doesn't double as an antenna.
keyNumbers: About 115 x 61 mm round the outside
Stands a fraction of a millimetre above the glass
Stainless steel is roughly three times as dense as aluminium
details.madeOf: Stainless steel, polished to a mirror finish. Steel is much harder and tougher than aluminium, which suits the edge that takes the most knocks.

parts.name: Stainless steel bezel

parts.description: Curved aluminium walls round the edge, part of the shell that holds the screen, boards and battery.

details.didYouKnow: At 11.6 mm the original iPhone felt thin for its day; a decade later, the iPhone X was under 8 mm thick despite having a much bigger screen.
details.howItWorks: The curved sides are part of the aluminium shell that everything else sits in. The logic board, battery and display are fixed inside it, and the buttons, switch and connectors poke through holes in its walls. A gently rounded edge made the phone more comfortable to hold than the boxy phones of the time.
keyNumbers: Aluminium is roughly a third as dense as steel
Corners rounded to about a 1 cm radius
details.madeOf: Aluminium, shaped and machined, then anodised to give a hard, coloured surface. Aluminium is light and stiff, but it blocks radio waves, which is why the bottom of the back had to be plastic.

parts.name: Aluminium case sides

parts.description: Anodised aluminium covering most of the back, with a hole for the camera lens.

details.didYouKnow: The silver-and-black two-tone back was dropped the next year: the iPhone 3G had an all-plastic back, partly because plastic let radio signals out all over.
details.howItWorks: The back plate makes up most of the outside and protects the battery and logic board. A small hole near the top corner lets the camera see out. Its job is mainly to look good and feel solid, while radio signals leave through the plastic strip at the bottom and the glass at the front.
keyNumbers: Covers roughly three quarters of the back
Anodised layer typically 10 to 25 micrometres thick
Back is flat, with curved edges
details.madeOf: Anodised aluminium in a silver-grey finish, with an Apple logo and lettering on the back. Anodising grows a hard layer of aluminium oxide out of the metal itself rather than painting it.

parts.name: Aluminium back

parts.description: Black plastic strip across the bottom of the back that lets radio signals through to the antennas behind it.

details.didYouKnow: The same problem still shapes phones today: metal-bodied phones have thin plastic lines cut across their frames so their antennas can talk to the network.
details.howItWorks: Metal reflects radio waves, so antennas sealed inside an aluminium box would barely work. The phone's antennas for the mobile network, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth sit behind this black strip at the bottom, where radio signals can pass through plastic. It clips onto the rest of the case and matches the curve of the aluminium.
keyNumbers: Covers the whole width of the back
Lets through radio signals from about 850 MHz to 2.4 GHz
details.madeOf: Black plastic, moulded to the shape of the case. Plastic doesn't conduct electricity, so it lets radio waves through.

parts.name: Antenna cover

parts.description: Button on the top edge that locks and wakes the phone; held down, it turns it off.

details.didYouKnow: Slide to unlock, the gesture that followed waking the phone, was one of the touches Jobs demonstrated on stage in 2007; it made sure the phone couldn't be unlocked by accident in a pocket.
details.howItWorks: A short press turns the screen off and locks the phone, or wakes it to the lock screen, where you slid your finger across the glass to unlock. Holding it for a few seconds brings up a slider to power the phone off. Holding it together with the home button forces a restart, or takes a screenshot on later software.
keyNumbers: Hold for about 2 to 3 seconds to power off
On the top edge, on the right as you face the screen
details.madeOf: A plastic cap over a small dome switch on a flex cable inside the top edge.

parts.name: Sleep/wake button

parts.description: Tray on the top edge, opened with a pin, holding the mini-SIM that tied the phone to its carrier.

details.didYouKnow: Within weeks of launch, hackers found ways to unlock the iPhone for other carriers' SIM cards, starting years of cat-and-mouse with Apple's software updates.
details.howItWorks: Pushing a straightened paper clip into the small hole pops the tray out. The mini-SIM card in it carries a tiny chip that proves to the network who you are, and its gold contacts press against springy contacts on the logic board. At launch, the iPhone only worked on one network in each country, such as AT&T in the United States.
keyNumbers: One carrier per country at launch
details.madeOf: Metal tray with a plastic SIM card inside. The tray sits flush with the top edge.

parts.name: SIM tray

parts.description: Button on the left side for turning the volume up.

details.didYouKnow: Using volume up as a camera shutter didn't arrive until iOS 5 in 2011, four years after the original iPhone came out.
details.howItWorks: The button presses a dome switch on a flex cable, which tells the processor to turn up whatever is playing: the ringer, music, or the other person on a call. An on-screen volume picture appears to show the level. Each button has its own switch, but they share one cable inside.
keyNumbers: Rated for many thousands of presses
details.madeOf: A small plastic cap over a stainless steel dome switch.

parts.name: Volume up button

parts.description: Button for turning the volume down.

details.didYouKnow: The original iPhone's earphones came with a single-click squeeze button on the cable for answering calls and pausing music, but no volume buttons.
details.howItWorks: This button lowers the volume, and turned all the way down it silences sounds from apps but not alarms. Like volume up, it simply closes a dome switch and leaves the rest to software. With no headphone volume control on many earphones of the time, these buttons did most of the work.
keyNumbers: On the left side, below volume up
details.madeOf: A small plastic cap over a stainless steel dome switch, on the same flex cable as volume up.

parts.name: Volume down button

parts.description: Small physical switch above the volume buttons that silences the ringer without looking at the screen.

details.didYouKnow: The ring/silent switch stayed on iPhones for 16 years until the iPhone 15 Pro replaced it with a programmable Action button in 2023.
details.howItWorks: Flicking the switch moves a tiny slider over a contact, and the phone silences its ringer and alert sounds while still vibrating. Because it's a real switch, you can feel whether it's on or off in a pocket without looking. When it's set to silent, a strip of orange paint shows in the slot.
details.madeOf: A small plastic slider in a slot in the aluminium side, over a switch on the button flex cable.

parts.name: Ring/silent switch

parts.description: Circuit board in the top half of the phone carrying the processor, memory and every radio.

details.didYouKnow: The battery being soldered to the board, rather than plugged in, caused a stir in 2007; replacing it meant sending the phone to Apple.
details.howItWorks: The logic board connects the processor, memory, storage and radio chips through copper wiring hidden in many thin layers. Flex cables plug into it from the display, touch sensor, camera and buttons, and the battery is soldered directly to it. Metal shields cover the radio chips so they don't interfere with each other or with the rest of the phone.
keyNumbers: Fits in the top half of the phone
details.madeOf: Layers of glass-fibre-reinforced epoxy with copper wiring between them, joined by tiny drilled holes. Chips are soldered on with lead-free solder.

parts.name: Logic board

parts.description: Samsung-made ARM processor running at 412 MHz, with 128 MB of memory stacked on top of it.

details.didYouKnow: The software at launch was simply called OS X, the same name as Apple's Mac system; it wasn't named iPhone OS until 2008, and iOS until 2010.
details.howItWorks: The processor runs the operating system and every app, while a small built-in graphics unit draws the smooth scrolling and animations that made the iPhone feel fast. It runs at a lower speed than its design allows, to save battery. The memory chip is stacked directly on top, a trick called package-on-package that saves board space and shortens the path for data.
details.madeOf: A silicon chip built by Samsung around an ARM11 processor core and a PowerVR graphics core, sealed in a package under the memory chip.

parts.name: Processor & memory

parts.description: Flash memory chip holding 4 or 8 GB of songs, photos and the phone's software.

details.didYouKnow: The 4 GB model was discontinued after just a few months, when Apple cut the 8 GB model's price from $599 to $399 in September 2007.
details.howItWorks: Flash memory stores data as charge trapped in billions of tiny cells, so it keeps your songs, photos and settings when the battery is flat. The iPhone used it like the iPod nano did, with no moving parts, so it wasn't damaged by drops the way a tiny hard disk could be. Part of it holds the operating system itself.
keyNumbers: Holds roughly 1,000 to 2,000 songs on the 8 GB model
details.madeOf: Samsung NAND flash memory chips in a single package. Flash is silicon with a special floating layer that holds charge for years.

parts.name: Flash storage

parts.description: Infineon chip that talks to the GSM and EDGE network on four frequency bands; there was no 3G.

details.didYouKnow: Leaving out 3G was the original iPhone's most criticised omission; Apple said 3G chips used too much battery, and added 3G a year later in the iPhone 3G.
details.howItWorks: This chip handles phone calls, text messages and mobile data, turning them into radio signals and back. It worked on GSM networks, with EDGE for data, on four frequency bands so the phone could work in most countries. Separate power amplifiers boost the signal before it reaches the antenna behind the black strip.
keyNumbers: EDGE data typically around 100 to 200 kbps
details.madeOf: A silicon chip from Infineon, paired with a separate radio transceiver, power amplifiers and filters.

parts.name: Phone radio chip

parts.description: Marvell chip for 802.11b/g Wi-Fi, much faster than the phone network for browsing at home.

details.didYouKnow: The original iPhone had no GPS chip; its Maps app guessed your position from nearby Wi-Fi networks and phone masts, a feature added in a software update in January 2008.
details.howItWorks: The Wi-Fi chip connects to home and office networks, which were far faster than the EDGE mobile network. Whenever a known network was in range, the phone switched to it automatically for browsing, email and the YouTube app. It shares the antennas behind the plastic strip with the Bluetooth chip.
details.madeOf: A silicon radio chip from Marvell, with its own small shield on the logic board.

parts.name: Wi-Fi chip

parts.description: Small CSR chip for Bluetooth 2.0, used at launch mainly for wireless headsets.

details.didYouKnow: Apple sold a tiny Bluetooth headset alongside the original iPhone, with a dock that charged the headset and the phone at the same time.
details.howItWorks: The Bluetooth chip links short-range accessories by radio. At launch it supported wireless headsets and car kits for calls, but not wireless stereo music or file transfers. It shares an antenna with Wi-Fi, since both work at 2.4 GHz.
details.madeOf: A small silicon radio chip from CSR, a British company that supplied Bluetooth chips for many phones of the time.

parts.name: Bluetooth chip

parts.description: Tiny motion sensor that feels which way is down, so the picture turns when you rotate the phone.

details.didYouKnow: Once the App Store opened in 2008, the accelerometer turned the iPhone into a game controller, with tilt-to-steer games that a stylus or keypad could never have managed.
details.howItWorks: Inside the chip, a tiny silicon weight hangs on springs and shifts slightly when the phone tilts or moves. The chip measures that shift as a change in electrical capacitance in three directions, which tells the phone which way gravity is pulling. Turn the phone sideways and the browser, photos and iPod's Cover Flow rotate to fill the screen.
keyNumbers: Range of about plus or minus 2 g
details.madeOf: A MEMS (micro-electromechanical system) chip: microscopic moving parts carved from silicon, sealed in a plastic package.

parts.name: Accelerometer

parts.description: Tiny motor that spins an off-centre weight to make the phone buzz when it's on silent.

details.didYouKnow: From the iPhone 6s onwards, Apple replaced the spinning motor with the Taptic Engine, a weight that slides back and forth, which can tap sharply instead of just buzzing.
details.howItWorks: A tiny electric motor spins a half-moon-shaped weight on its shaft. Because the weight is off-centre, the whole phone shakes as it spins, giving a buzz you can feel in a pocket. It runs when a call comes in on silent and in some alerts.
keyNumbers: Spins thousands of times a minute
Draws a small fraction of a watt
details.madeOf: A small DC motor with copper windings and magnets in a steel can, with a heavy tungsten or brass weight on the shaft.

parts.name: Vibration motor

parts.description: Lithium-ion polymer battery of 1,400 mAh, soldered to the board rather than swappable.

details.didYouKnow: Shortly before launch, Apple announced that the promised talk time had gone up from 5 to 8 hours.
details.howItWorks: Lithium ions move from one electrode to the other through an electrolyte as the battery discharges, and are pushed back when it's charged. A small protection circuit stops it being over-charged or drained too far. Because the battery was soldered in, Apple ran a replacement service rather than letting owners swap it themselves.
keyNumbers: Up to about 8 hours of talk time
Up to about 250 hours on standby
details.madeOf: A lithium-ion polymer cell: thin layers of graphite and a lithium metal oxide with a gel-like electrolyte, sealed in a flexible pouch.

parts.name: Battery

parts.description: The wide iPod connector on the bottom edge, used for charging, syncing with iTunes and speaker docks.

details.didYouKnow: Not every iPod accessory worked: some speakers buzzed from interference by the iPhone's phone radio, and the phone would suggest switching on airplane mode to stop it.
details.howItWorks: The wide connector carried power for charging, USB data for syncing with iTunes on a computer, and analogue audio and video out to speaker docks and TVs. Its 30 contacts made it work with the huge range of iPod accessories already on sale. The phone had to be plugged into a computer and activated through iTunes before it could be used.
details.madeOf: Gold-plated metal contacts held in a plastic body, inside a stainless steel shell soldered to a flex cable.

parts.name: 30-pin dock connector

parts.description: Flexible circuit of copper shapes under the black cover; this is why the bottom of the back isn't metal.

details.didYouKnow: A meandering trace lets a resonant length of conductor fit in a small space, which is why phone antennas look like squiggles rather than rods.
details.howItWorks: An antenna is a conductor shaped so that radio waves of a certain length set currents flowing in it. Metal would block those waves, so the antennas lie behind the plastic end of the phone. Thin coaxial cable carries their signals up to the radio chips at the far end of the phone.
keyNumbers: GSM and EDGE on four frequency bands
Covers roughly the bottom fifth of the phone
details.madeOf: Copper shapes on a thin flexible plastic film, stuck to the inside of the black cover or a carrier behind it, with a miniature coaxial lead.

parts.name: Antenna flex

parts.description: Fixed-focus camera in the top corner of the back; it took still photos only, with no flash and no video.

details.didYouKnow: Video recording only came to iPhones with the iPhone 3GS in 2009, and a front camera for FaceTime with the iPhone 4 in 2010.
details.howItWorks: A small plastic lens focuses light onto an image sensor, which turns it into a grid of brightness and colour readings. The lens is fixed, so everything from about arm's length to the horizon is roughly in focus, and there's no zoom, flash or autofocus. Photos appeared in the Photos app and could be emailed or synced to a computer, but the camera couldn't record video.
details.madeOf: A stack of moulded plastic lenses in a small barrel over a CMOS silicon image sensor, behind a clear window in the aluminium back.

parts.name: 2-megapixel camera

parts.description: Mono speaker behind the left grille on the bottom edge, for the ringtone, music and speakerphone.

details.didYouKnow: The two grilles either side of the dock connector look like a pair of speakers, but only the left one holds a speaker; the right one hides the microphone.
details.howItWorks: A small voice coil and magnet push a diaphragm to make sound, inside a sealed plastic box that acts like a tiny speaker cabinet to strengthen the bass. It plays ringtones, alerts, speakerphone calls and music without headphones. Sound leaves through the grille on the left of the dock connector.
keyNumbers: Grille left of the dock connector
Loud enough for speakerphone calls across a desk
details.madeOf: A thin diaphragm, copper voice coil and neodymium magnet in a moulded plastic enclosure, behind a fine metal mesh.

parts.name: Loudspeaker

parts.description: Single microphone behind the right grille on the bottom edge, close to your mouth on a call.

details.didYouKnow: From the iPhone 4 onwards, a second microphone at the top listened to the background so the phone could subtract it from your voice.
details.howItWorks: A thin diaphragm moves with the air pressure of your voice, changing a tiny electrical charge that a chip turns into a signal for the phone call. It sits at the bottom of the phone, close to your mouth. With only one microphone, the original iPhone couldn't cancel background noise the way later phones with several microphones could.
keyNumbers: Grille right of the dock connector
Picks up roughly the range of a human voice
details.madeOf: A small electret microphone capsule: a permanently charged plastic film and a metal plate, in a metal can sealed into a rubber boot.

parts.name: Microphone

parts.description: 3.5 mm socket on the top edge, set so deep in the case that many headphone plugs needed an adapter.

details.didYouKnow: The jack sat at the bottom of a narrow, deep hole, so many headphones with chunky plugs didn't reach it, and accessory makers quickly sold small adapters to fix it.
details.howItWorks: The socket's springy contacts touch the rings on a headphone plug, carrying left and right audio and, through a fourth contact, the signal from the earphones' microphone and button. The phone senses when a plug goes in and switches sound away from the loudspeaker.
keyNumbers: Four contacts: left, right, ground and microphone
details.madeOf: Metal spring contacts held in a plastic housing, mounted at the end of a flex cable inside the top edge.

parts.name: Headphone jack

summary: The first iPhone, from 2007: a 3.5-inch multi-touch screen under glass, a chrome bezel, an aluminium back with a black plastic window for the antennas, and a small computer, radios and battery packed inside.
